full.text: Viruses are very small, non-cellular infectious particles that reproduce only inside living host cells.

items: A core of nucleic acid: DNA or RNA, never both
Some have a lipid *envelope* from the host membrane

full.text: Attachment to the host, injection of nucleic acid, replication of viral parts using the host's machinery, assembly of new viruses and lysis of the host cell to release them.
In the lysogenic cycle the viral DNA joins the host chromosome and is copied with it until it becomes active.
Antibiotics do not work against viruses because viruses have no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolism of their own.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: State that viruses can be crystallised and have no metabolism, which places them on the border of living and non-living.

items: Lytic: attach, inject, replicate, assemble, lyse
Lysogenic: viral DNA in host chromosome

full.text: A bacterial population in a closed culture shows four phases of growth.

items: Lag phase: cells adjust, little division
Log (exponential) phase: rapid division by binary fission
Stationary phase: division rate equals death rate as nutrients run out and wastes build up
Death (decline) phase: more cells die than are formed

full.text: The time taken for a bacterial population to double.

items: Physical: heat (autoclaving at 121 C), refrigeration, drying, radiation, filtration
Antibiotics act on bacteria inside the body

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: Sterilisation kills all microorganisms including spores; disinfection only reduces their number.

items: Stationary: nutrients run out, wastes build up

full.text: Microorganisms are used to make many useful products.

items: Yeast (Saccharomyces): bread, alcoholic drinks by fermentation
Lactobacillus: yoghurt, curd and cheese by lactic acid fermentation
Genetically modified bacteria: insulin and other proteins

full.text: Anaerobic breakdown of organic substances by microorganisms, producing useful products such as ethanol or lactic acid.
Industrial production uses large fermenters with controlled temperature, pH, oxygen and nutrient supply, under aseptic conditions.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: Name the microbe together with the product. Many answers lose marks by naming only the product.

written.stem: Describe the four phases of bacterial growth in a closed culture.
written.model_answer: In the lag phase cells adjust and make enzymes with little division. In the log phase they divide rapidly by binary fission. In the stationary phase nutrients run out and wastes build up so division equals death. In the death phase more cells die than are produced.

written.stem: Describe the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage.
written.model_answer: The phage attaches to the bacterial cell and injects its DNA. The viral DNA takes over the host to make viral nucleic acid and proteins. New phages are assembled and the host cell bursts (lysis), releasing them.

points.text: Replication and assembly using the host

written.stem: Name four useful products made by microorganisms and the microorganism used for each.
written.model_answer: Bread and alcohol by yeast (Saccharomyces); yoghurt by Lactobacillus; penicillin by Penicillium; citric acid by Aspergillus; insulin by genetically modified bacteria.

points.text: Aspergillus or GM bacteria with product

written.stem: Explain three steps of aseptic technique used when transferring bacteria.
written.model_answer: Sterilise the inoculating loop by flaming until red hot and let it cool; flame the neck of the culture bottle when opening and closing it; lift the lid of the Petri dish only slightly and work near a Bunsen flame to reduce contamination.

points.text: Open Petri dish lid only slightly

written.stem: Describe the cause, transmission and control of dengue fever and tuberculosis.
written.model_answer: Dengue is caused by the dengue virus and spread by the bite of Aedes mosquitoes; it is controlled by removing breeding places, using repellents and nets. Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis and spread through air droplets from coughing; it is controlled by BCG vaccination, early diagnosis and a full course of antibiotics.

written.stem: Discuss the importance of microorganisms in agriculture and the environment.
written.model_answer: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead matter. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium and cyanobacteria such as Anabaena increase soil nitrogen and act as biofertilisers. Microbes are used in composting and biogas production and in bioremediation of pollutants such as oil. Some microbes are used as biopesticides, such as Bacillus thuringiensis. Some cause plant diseases.

ask.question: Why don't antibiotics work on viruses?
ask.answer: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures and processes such as cell walls and bacterial ribosomes. Viruses have no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolism of their own, so antibiotics cannot affect them.

ask.question: What are the phases of bacterial growth?
ask.answer: In a closed culture there is a lag phase, a log (exponential) phase, a stationary phase when nutrients run out and wastes build up, and a death phase.

ask.question: How is yoghurt made?
ask.answer: Milk is heated, cooled and inoculated with lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus. They ferment lactose to lactic acid, which lowers the pH and makes the milk proteins thicken.

ask.question: How is dengue spread?
ask.answer: Dengue is caused by a virus spread by the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. Removing water where mosquitoes breed is the main way to control it.

ask.question: What is a bacteriophage?
ask.answer: A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria. It injects its nucleic acid into the bacterium and may reproduce by the lytic cycle, bursting the cell, or join the host DNA in the lysogenic cycle.
